title: How Antizionism’s Libels Against Israel Mirror the Prelude to the Rwandan Genocide
summary: The author summarizes a Wall Street Journal essay by Adam Louis-Klein arguing that accusations of genocide against Israel parallel Hutu propaganda that falsely accused Tutsis of genocide before 1994. It contends that the 'settler-colonial' framing mirrors colonial-era 'Hamitic' racial myths and calls for exposing this pattern while still permitting critique of specific Israeli policies.
stance: critical of antizionism and genocide accusations against Israel
relevance_reason: The post summarizes an essay arguing that genocide accusations against Israel and the settler-colonial framing function as an antizionist inversion tactic, directly addressing antizionist rhetoric and ideology.

title: How to Punish a "Zionist"
summary: Using sarcasm, the author walks through the core antizionist claims (whiteness, settler-colonialism, supremacy, apartheid, genocide) and rebuts each by pointing to historical facts, Soviet and UN origins, and antisemitic precedents. The author concludes that antizionism functions as classical antisemitism with a record of harm to Jewish communities.
stance: critical of antizionism (satirical)
relevance_reason: The post is a sustained satirical dissection of antizionist rhetoric, tropes, and their historical and institutional roots.

title: This Essay Has No Right to Exist
summary: The author presents a lyrical, literary essay tracing antizionism as the latest form of ancient Jew-hatred, in which society projects its guilt onto Jews through libels like colonizer, genocide, and baby-killer. Citing recent attacks and figures from politics, media, and entertainment, the author argues that Jews must stop turning their gaze inward and instead name and confront antizionism directly.
stance: strongly opposed to antizionism, framing it as a hate movement and urging Jews to name it
relevance_reason: The essay is entirely about antizionism as a continuation of historical Jew-hatred, covering its rhetoric, institutions, cultural figures, and the Jewish response.

title: The ADL is Confusing Activism with Marketing (Dispatch #15)
summary: The author argues that the ADL has shifted from activist defense of Jews to marketing and brand-management logic, relying on polling and agreeable messaging rather than confronting antizionism as a hate movement. The author calls for the ADL to return to activist logic and notes that grassroots Jews are bearing the burden in the meantime.
stance: critical of the ADL's approach; advocates confrontational activism against antizionism
relevance_reason: The post centers on how Jewish organizations, specifically the ADL, respond to antizionism, and frames antizionism as a hate movement.

title: Yesterday We Stood Up — This Is Only the Beginning
summary: The author reports on a May 14, 2026 rally outside the New York Times headquarters and argues that antizionism is an eliminationist hate movement and heir to Nazi, Soviet, and Arab propaganda. The post lists five actions supporters can take and reproduces Adam Louis-Klein's speech condemning antizionists and media institutions.
stance: strongly opposed to antizionism; advocacy for a movement against it
relevance_reason: The post is an organizational report and speech centered on antizionism as a hate movement, including its Soviet and Middle Eastern lineage and its media and institutional manifestations.

title: End Antizionism Denial Now (Dispatch #14)
summary: The author argues that antizionism is a coherent, eliminationist hate movement and that widespread denial of this, from Jewish anti-Zionists, mainstream Jewish institutions, and political figures, enables it. He cites Iranian attacks and plots, the Beinart and Sanders statements, and examples of campus and cultural antizionism, and calls for naming antizionism plainly and confronting it.
stance: strongly critical of antizionism and of those who deny or downplay it
relevance_reason: The post is centrally about antizionism, framing it as an eliminationist hate movement and critiquing those who deny or minimize it.

title: Meet the Architects of Academic Antizionism (Dispatch #13)
summary: The author traces a roughly century-long genealogy of antizionism in academia, from Soviet and Arab nationalist propaganda through postcolonial theory and settler-colonial theory to the construction of the genocide libel. The dispatch names key scholars at each stage and argues they embedded antizionist ideology in academic institutions, with several Jewish or Israeli-born figures tokenized for added legitimacy.
stance: strongly critical of antizionism and the scholars who developed and spread it
relevance_reason: The post is a genealogical mapping of antizionism as an ideology and its institutionalization in the academy, squarely on topic.

title: Antizionism Is Not Jewish Anti-Zionism (Dispatch #12)
summary: The author argues that conflating pre-1948 Jewish anti-Zionism, a set of intra-Jewish debates, with contemporary antizionism, which he characterizes as a hate ideology denying Jews the right to political self-determination, gives the latter cover and endangers Jewish communities. He urges hyphenation-based terminological precision, naming antizionism as hate, and asking non-Jews for help in interrupting it.
stance: strongly critical of antizionism; advocates terminological precision and stigmatizing it as a hate movement
relevance_reason: The post is an essay centrally about antizionism, distinguishing it from historical Jewish anti-Zionism and examining its genealogy, rhetoric, and consequences.

title: Dispatch #11: Apartheid Week Is Coming. Are We Ready?
summary: The author argues that Israeli Apartheid Week and the apartheid charge against Israel derive from anti-Judaic theology, Arab nationalist and Soviet propaganda, and the 2001 Durban conference, and that the label is historically inaccurate, selectively applied, and used to justify boycotts and exclusion of Jews and Israelis. He calls for coordinated public, campus, and social media counter-campaigns ahead of this year's Apartheid Week.
stance: critical of Israeli Apartheid Week and the apartheid accusation; advocacy for organized counter-response
relevance_reason: The post is substantially about Israeli Apartheid Week, the apartheid libel, its theological and Soviet/Arab origins, and BDS tactics, and calls for a response.

title: Dispatch #10: How Jewish Discourse Misdiagnoses Antizionism
summary: The author argues that Jewish discourse repeatedly misdiagnoses antizionism through seven rhetorical habits, including 'cross the line' framing, the 'mask' metaphor, hyphenating 'anti-Zionism,' and claiming 'it's not about Israel.' He contends these habits fold antizionism into older forms of antisemitism rather than treating it as a distinct ideology aimed at eliminating Israel and purging those labeled 'Zionists,' and he proposes clearer language instead.
stance: critical of Jewish communal discourse; argues antizionism is a distinct hate ideology
relevance_reason: The post is a sustained analysis of how Jewish discourse describes and mislabels antizionism, arguing it is a distinct ideology and hate movement.

title: Dispatch #9: Why the Jewish World Is Unprepared for the U.S. Midterm Elections—and How to Fix It
summary: The author argues that antizionism is mainstreaming across the American left and increasingly the right, comparing current purges of Jews labeled "Zionists" to earlier MENA, Soviet, and Polish campaigns. He contends that antizionism remains invisible to the public and urges Jewish organizations to educate about it and press political candidates with a provided question list before the midterms.
stance: critical of antizionism; advocacy for Jewish organizations to confront it
relevance_reason: The post is centrally about antizionism as a hate movement, its mainstreaming in left- and right-wing politics, its historical precedents, and how Jewish organizations should respond ahead of U.S. elections.

title: Dispatch #8: Why Physical Self-Defense Is Not a Politics
summary: The author argues that the turn toward armed self-defense after the Bondi Hanukkah massacre reflects Jewish civic retreat, and that Jewish organizations have failed for decades to name antizionism as the ideology driving anti-Jewish hate. He contends antizionism is a libel-narrative system with Nazi-Arab, Soviet, and settler-colonial roots that operates across left and right, and calls for precise public campaigns against it.
stance: critical of Jewish institutional response; advocates naming and confronting antizionism as a hate movement
relevance_reason: The post's central argument is that Jewish institutions have failed to name and combat antizionism as a hate ideology, tracing its genealogy and consequences.

title: Dispatch #7: How the ADL’s Messaging Guidelines Undermine Jewish Self-Defense
summary: The author argues that the ADL's 2024 messaging guidelines, which discourage using the word antizionism and emphasize Jewish relatability and ally messengers, undermine Jewish self-defense. He proposes the MAAZ framework of principles for speaking plainly, starting with naming antizionism as a distinct ideology separate from classical antisemitism and religious antijudaism.
stance: critical of the ADL's messaging approach; advocates naming antizionism as a hate movement
relevance_reason: The post is centrally about antizionism: it critiques the ADL's guidelines for avoiding the term, defines antizionism as a distinct hate movement, and traces its history and libels.

title: Dispatch #6: The Political Rationalization of Anti-Jewish Hate
summary: The author argues that every era justifies anti-Jewish hatred as a political response to supposed Jewish offenses, tracing this from medieval libels through Dreyfus and Kristallnacht to the Amsterdam attacks and the Boulder firebombing. He contends that contemporary antizionist narratives (colonizer, apartheid, genocide) are libels in the same lineage, and that softening our language for them obscures the pattern.
stance: critical of antizionism and of commentators who frame anti-Jewish violence as 'political'
relevance_reason: The essay directly analyzes antizionism as a continuation of historical anti-Jewish libels and argues that framing anti-Jewish violence as 'political' is the mechanism by which the hatred justifies itself.

title: Dispatch #4: Beyond Meteorological Discourse
summary: The author argues that Jewish responses to antizionism are stuck in defensive self-scrutiny and vague 'meteorological' language that hides perpetrators. He calls for a Jewish civil-rights consciousness with a precise vocabulary naming antizionist slurs, libels, conspiracies, exclusion, harassment and violence, and he examines why Jews resist naming antizionism.
stance: critical of antizionism and of Jewish communal responses that avoid naming it
relevance_reason: The post is an extended analysis of antizionism as an ideology and of how Jewish communities respond to it, including a typology of antizionist harms.

title: Dispatch #3: The Genealogy of Antizionist Hate
summary: The author traces antizionism from Lenin and the Yevsektsiya through Soviet propaganda, into Arab nationalism and expulsions of Jews from the Middle East, and then into Western academia and activism, culminating in its post-October 7 surge. The author argues it is a coherent ideology of exclusion that should be critically studied, and the post also includes a call for personal stories for a podcast series.
stance: critical of antizionism, framing it as a hate ideology
relevance_reason: The post is a genealogy of antizionism, tracing its Soviet, Arab-nationalist, and Western academic/activist forms and its post-October 7 mainstreaming.

title: Dispatch #2: The Cycle of Libel
summary: The author argues that anti-Jewish hatred renews itself through a four-stage cycle of libel, stigma, violence, and denial, and that anti-Jewish libel should be understood as ideological abuse rather than answered point by point. The post cites a Toronto incident in which a masked mob confronted a Jewish woman and closes with calls to educate, engage, and join a sticker campaign.
stance: critical of antizionism, framing it as the contemporary form of anti-Jewish libel
relevance_reason: The post frames antizionism as the latest iteration of a recurring anti-Jewish libel cycle and illustrates it with a contemporary antizionist mob incident and the genocide libel.

title: Welcome to the Movement Against Antizionism (MAAZ)
summary: The author introduces the Movement Against Antizionism and, drawing on Naya Lekht's framework, argues that Jew-hatred has taken three forms: religious antijudaism, racial antisemitism, and nation-based antizionism. The post urges precise naming of antizionism, advises focusing on uncommitted audiences rather than committed ideologues, and offers calls to action and an upcoming CUNY lecture announcement.
stance: strongly critical of antizionism, framing it as a hate ideology and the third era of Jew-hatred
relevance_reason: The post is an inaugural dispatch defining antizionism as a form of Jew-hatred and presenting a framework for understanding and responding to it.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: Combatting Municipal Antizionism
summary: The author argues that the most effective way to defeat municipal anti-Israel resolutions is to push pro-peace resolutions rather than fight over narratives. This would focus officials on ordinary Palestinians and Israelis and on international peace frameworks, and casts radical antizionists as favoring perpetual war.
stance: advocacy strategy; opposes municipal anti-Israel resolutions
relevance_reason: The post is a strategy note on how to counter local anti-Israel resolutions and the oppressor/colonialism/apartheid/genocide narrative driving them.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Rebecca Nesvet: “Profiles and Cowardice: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History and the New York Public Library”
summary: The author argues that Benjamin Moser's 'Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History' is riddled with hyperbole, misinformation, and disingenuous use of evidence, including profiles of subjects who are not clearly Jewish or who held contradictory views. The author also contends that the New York Public Library, which hosted Moser as a Cullman Fellow, has urgent questions to answer about the book.
stance: critical of Moser's book and of the New York Public Library's role in its production
relevance_reason: The post is a critical review of Benjamin Moser's book 'Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History', directly examining antizionist ideology, its Jewish proponents, and the scholarly standards of the book.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Simon Lucas: “The ‘Toxic Colonialism’ that Wasn’t”
summary: The author argues that a Journal of Medical Ethics editorial accusing Israel of 'toxic colonialism' in Gaza relies on selective evidence, misquoted figures, and assumptions that assign guilt in advance, ignoring alternative explanations such as organizational failures and uncoordinated donations via Egypt. He contends this exemplifies ideological bias and weak evidentiary standards in contemporary bioethics.
stance: critical of the 'toxic colonialism' framing and of bioethics scholarship on Israel
relevance_reason: The essay critiques a Journal of Medical Ethics editorial that frames medical aid in Gaza as 'toxic colonialism,' directly addressing antizionist rhetoric and ideological bias in bioethics.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Simon Lucas, “Morbus Israel—case notes on a discipline in exitus”
summary: The author argues, through satire, thought experiments, and case studies from bioethics and philosophy journals, that antizionism has corrupted editorial standards and moral reasoning in the discipline. He presents a ten-part diagnostic manual of rhetorical and scholarly pathologies and contends the field has become a vehicle for delegitimizing Israel and fostering antisemitic double standards.
stance: strongly critical of antizionism in academic philosophy and bioethics
relevance_reason: The essay directly analyzes antizionism's penetration of academic moral philosophy and bioethics journals, its rhetoric, and its link to antisemitic double standards.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Victoria Villar: “The New Fangled Myth of the ‘Far Right’”
summary: The author argues that 'far right' is a media and political myth deployed mainly by the left to polarize societies, stigmatize dissent, and obscure issues such as crime, immigration, Islamism, and antisemitism. She extends the argument to Western treatment of Israel and Palestine, claiming the Palestinian cause is mythologized to cast Palestinians as perpetual victims and Israel as an archetypal oppressor.
stance: critical of the left, mainstream media, and the 'far right' label; sympathetic to Israel
relevance_reason: The essay devotes substantial space to the Western left-Islamist alliance, post-October 7 antisemitism, and the mythologizing of the Palestinian cause and terms like 'Palestine' and 'intifada', though its main thesis concerns the 'far right' label.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Jonathan Sacerdoti: Why the West Should be Suspicious of Islam
summary: The author, in a transcript of his Oxford Union debate remarks, argues the West should be suspicious of Islam, citing terror attacks, the Rushdie affair, the Muslim Brotherhood's 'civilizational jihad' strategy, and a history of Islamic conquest and dhimmi subjugation. He contends that people ignore their suspicions out of fear of being branded racist, and urges Western audiences to apply the same scrutiny to Islam as to any other ideology.
stance: Strongly critical of Islam and Islamism; advocates Western suspicion of it
relevance_reason: The post is an Oxford Union debate speech arguing the West should be suspicious of Islam, centered on Islamist terrorism, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Islamic supremacism, with only passing references to Jewish victims and no direct engagement with antizionism.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Jeffrey Malkan, "The Fall of Jewish Columbia"
summary: The author argues that Columbia University's faculty and students, driven by critical race theory and a settler-colonial worldview, have turned the campus against Jews and Israel, culminating in the 2024 encampments and celebration of October 7. He frames this as a betrayal of academic vocation, comparable to the treason of German intellectuals in the 1920s, and as a revival of Jewish scapegoating.
stance: critical of Columbia faculty and campus antizionism
relevance_reason: The essay centrally examines campus antizionism at Columbia, its ideological roots in critical race theory and settler-colonial framing, and the faculty's role in it.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Jones and Gisle: "The Antizionist Script: How Two Strangers Reached the Same Conclusion"
summary: Two authors, Jones and Gisle, each recount how they came to antizionism through academia and punk/anarchist activism, and how October 7th led them away from it. They argue the movement uses an identical script of 'colonizer, apartheid, genocide', drawn from Said, Fanon, Wolfe and others, and that it shuts out dissenters and ultimately targets Jews.
stance: critical of antizionism; first-person accounts of leaving it
relevance_reason: The post is a personal and analytical account of how two former antizionists were recruited into, and later left, the antizionist worldview, examining its vocabulary, intellectual sources, and effects.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Barry Finger, "Review of Molly Crabapple, 'Here Where We Live Is Our Country' (Random House, 2026)"
summary: The author reviews Molly Crabapple's book, which holds up the anti-Zionist Bund as a model for leftist Jews today, and argues she ignores Labor Zionism's critique of Bundism and the Bund's historical failures. He traces the socialist movement's indifference to Jewish survival and contends that both the Bund and Labor Zionists offered serious but competing programs for Jewish national survival.
stance: critical of Crabapple's Bundist anti-Zionism; sympathetic to Labor Zionism
relevance_reason: The review centers on the Bund's anti-Zionism, Crabapple's use of it as a model for contemporary anti-Zionist Jewish politics, and the socialist/Marxist history of the Jewish question and Zionism.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Toby Moneit: "Naming Antizionism Begets Claims of Islamophobia"
summary: The author, organizer of a Montreal college Holocaust symposium, describes a student complaint alleging that a talk on antizionism spread islamophobia, antisemitism and misinformation. She argues the complaint conflates Palestinian political symbols and political Islam with the religion of Islam, and that it is a DARVO tactic that reverses victim and offender.</br>
stance: critical of students' complaint and of deflecting claims of islamophobia; supportive of naming antizionism as hate
relevance_reason: The post is a firsthand account of a campus complaint triggered by a talk naming antizionism as a form of Jew hatred, and it directly addresses the rhetoric used to deflect that critique.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Ernest Sternberg: "Dog-Rape and Organ Harvesting: The Logic of Humanitarian Blood Libel"
summary: The author argues that claims of dog-rape and organ harvesting against Israel, such as Nicholas Kristof's reliance on Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, are modern blood libels, and shows the organ-theft claim is medically implausible. He contends that progressive humanitarianism now plays the role that race pseudoscience played in earlier antisemitism, serving as a respectable vehicle for demonizing Zionists.
stance: critical of antizionism and of humanitarian NGOs and media that amplify anti-Israel accusations
relevance_reason: The essay directly analyzes the ideology and rhetoric of antizionism, specifically how humanitarian discourse is used to spread blood-libel-style accusations against Israel.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Andrew Bostom: "Negating Islamic Antisemitism"
summary: The author argues that Loay Alshareef falsely claimed at a Toronto symposium that the Qur'an is free of antisemitism and that only some hadith are problematic. Citing Qur'anic commentators, hadith, and Islamic scholarship, he contends that Jew-hatred is doctrinally embedded in Islam, and he cites ADL survey data on antisemitism in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
stance: critical of Loay Alshareef and of what the author calls Muslim dissimulation about Islamic antisemitism
relevance_reason: The post critiques a speaker's remarks at a symposium against antizionism and argues that Islamic antisemitism rooted in Islamic scripture and tradition is a core driver of hostility toward Jews, a substantial topic within antizionism's ideological sources.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: On Jewish Education
summary: In an address at Frankel Jewish Academy, the author argues that antizionism is an ideology that distorts perception, as seen in campus celebrations of October 7, and that it must be fought as a cognitive war. He contends that Jewish day schools equip students with the history, tradition, and truth needed to resist campus hostility, drawing on his own cancellation experience.
stance: critical of antizionism as a delusional ideology; advocating Jewish education as the response
relevance_reason: The speech centers on antizionism as an ideology driving campus hostility and argues Jewish education is the remedy.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Simon Lucas, "Academic antizionism as secularized religious dogma"
summary: The author argues that contemporary academic antizionism functions as a secularized religious dogma, with mythic narratives, replacement theology, ritual confession, and heresy policing replacing empirical rigor and open inquiry. He contends this undermines the university's commitment to truth-seeking and suppresses dissent through publishing gatekeeping and social pressure.
stance: critical of academic antizionism
relevance_reason: The essay is wholly about academic antizionism, analyzing its rhetoric, narratives, and enforcement of orthodoxy in universities.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Russell Shalev: "A Bespoke Slur: Why 'Ethnocracy' is a Pseudo-Academic Weapon Against Israel"
summary: The author argues that 'ethnocracy' is a term coined specifically to delegitimize Israel and is applied selectively, since democracies like Greece and Estonia have comparable ethnic and diaspora ties. He also disputes claims of discriminatory Israeli land law and argues a Palestinian state would itself be an ethnostate.
stance: critical of the 'ethnocracy' concept and of antizionist double standards toward Israel
relevance_reason: The post directly analyzes and rebuts the 'ethnocracy'/'ethnostate' label as a delegitimizing antizionist rhetorical and pseudo-academic device.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Allen Zeesman: How Antisemitism Adapts to the Moral Language of Each Age
summary: The author, drawing on Jonathan Sacks, argues that antisemitism persists by adapting to the dominant moral language of each era (religious, national, racial, and now liberal discourse centered on power and justice). In the contemporary liberal age, he contends, it often takes the form of antizionism, in which Israel is classed as 'powerful' and judged asymmetrically.
stance: critical of antizionism as a modern form of antisemitism
relevance_reason: The essay directly analyzes antizionism as the contemporary form of antisemitism's adaptation to liberal moral language centered on power and justice.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: Despair or Hope in the Battle Against Academic Antizionism
summary: A reader describes the isolation and career risk of being a liberal Zionist in a humanities department where antizionism is the consensus, and doubts that writing makes a difference. Andrew Pessin replies that ICSA aims to flood academia with scholarship to move the silent middle, or at least go down fighting.
stance: critical of academic antizionism; personal account with a mix of despair and resolve
relevance_reason: The post centers on antizionism in academia, including BDS and genocide-libel consensus in the humanities and how to respond to it.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Erez Levin, "The Linguistic Shell Game"
summary: The author argues that 'antisemitism' has been diluted by overuse, while antizionism, which he says advocates dismantling Israel, has been sanitized as academic critique. He proposes a 'hierarchy of harm' that separates tropes and legitimate policy critique from eliminationist Jew-hatred and antizionism, and urges reserving the strongest condemnation for the latter.
stance: critical of antizionism and of the overuse of the term 'antisemitism'
relevance_reason: The post directly examines antizionism, arguing it is an eliminationist ideology that should be treated as a graver taboo than diluted 'antisemitism'.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Anonymous Guest Author: Reflections from a Jewish-American PhD Student
summary: A Jewish-American PhD student describes attending a lecture presenting antizionist claims as fact and the fear of speaking up in class. The author cautions that ICSA's 'saving the West' language and battle metaphors may reinforce the frameworks it opposes, and draws on scholarship on transnational advocacy networks.
stance: critical of academic antizionism, while offering constructive criticism of ICSA's 'saving the West' framing
relevance_reason: The post is a first-person account of encountering academic antizionism and antizionist libel in a graduate program, alongside a critique of how ICSA frames its mission.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Marcia Kupfer, "'Palestine'" as a geographic label in popular and academic histories"
summary: The author argues that after October 7, Western antizionist discourse turned 'Palestine' into both a totalizing moral cause and a trivialized meme, using 'context' and decolonization frames to negate Israeli victimhood. She contends this reproduces older Christian anti-Jewish supersessionist tropes, such as the 'Palestinian Jesus,' and conflates antizionism with exclusion of Jews in practice.
suggested_tags: American politics and the Democratic Party
stance: critical of antizionist discourse and the instrumentalization of 'Palestine'
relevance_reason: The post directly analyzes post-October 7 antizionist discourse, including the genocide libel, decolonization framing, and the use of 'Palestine' as a totalizing cause and meme.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Eric Daniel Buesing, "From Eugenics to Anti-Zionism: Elite Philanthropy and the Structural Marginalization of Jewish Self-Determination"
summary: The author argues, using Foucault's genealogical method, that the Ford, Rockefeller, Carnegie, and Mellon foundations have shifted from funding eugenics and immigration restriction aimed at Jews to funding BDS groups and decolonial academic pipelines that delegitimize Israel. The paper contends that the institutional effect on Jewish self-determination has stayed the same even as the ideological vocabulary changed.
stance: critical of elite philanthropic foundations; argues they exhibit structural antisemitism
relevance_reason: The essay is scholarly work on how major philanthropic foundations fund antizionist activism, BDS organizations, and decolonial academic frameworks targeting Israel's legitimacy.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Dan Burmawi, "The Re-Zionization of the West"
summary: The author argues that after 9/11 the West exonerated Islam via the 'Islamism' distinction, and that October 7 dropped that mask as Muslims and the radical left converged on Israel as the symbol of the West. He further contends that segments of the American right betrayed Israel out of cowardice, antisemitism, delusion, or money. A brief editorial introduction presents the author's book and institute as a contribution to the study of antizionism's Islamic dimension.
stance: strongly critical of Islam, the radical left, and anti-Israel voices on the right
relevance_reason: The essay directly analyzes how antizionism functions as a convergence point for Islamist and radical-left ideology after October 7, and criticizes right-wing figures who joined in demonizing Israel.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: From Cary Nelson, A Call for Contributors: "No Ivory Towers: Academic Disciplines Captured by Antizionism"
summary: Cary Nelson proposes a multi-author volume examining how various academic disciplines have been captured by hostility to Israel since 10/7, arguing that antizionist departments and disciplinary associations are the main organized force behind campus antizionism. He invites one-page proposals for essays on the history of antizionism within individual fields and professional associations.
stance: critical of antizionism in academic disciplines
relevance_reason: The post is a call for contributors to a multi-author volume on how academic disciplines have been captured by antizionism, directly addressing antizionism in the academy.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: A Good Debate for the Seder Table?
summary: The editor presents an exchange over Robert Goldberg's thesis that Amalek is the archetype of the anti-Zionist Jew. Elder of Ziyon argues Korach, the insider who weaponizes his Jewishness, is a better fit, while Goldberg replies that rabbinic sources show Korach sought only power and that Amalek's aim to block Jewish sovereignty better matches anti-Zionism.
stance: curated exchange; editor neutral, with Elder of Ziyon and Goldberg both critical of anti-Zionist Jews but disagreeing on the archetype
relevance_reason: The post presents a debate between two authors over the proper scriptural archetype (Amalek vs. Korach) for anti-Zionist Jews, directly engaging the ideology and rhetoric of antizionism among Jews.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Robert Goldberg, "Amalek: The Archetypal Anti-Zionist Jew"
summary: The author argues that Amalek functions as a transhistorical archetype for the antizionist Jew, with the Haggadah's Wicked Son as his internal form and modern Jewish antizionists as contemporary incarnations. He contends such positions threaten Jewish continuity and calls for an unapologetic affirmation of Zionism as integral to Jewish destiny.
stance: strongly critical of antizionism, especially antizionist Jews; pro-Zionist theological argument
relevance_reason: The essay is centrally about antizionism, framing the biblical figure of Amalek and the Haggadah's Wicked Son as archetypes of the antizionist Jew and discussing modern Jewish antizionists such as Buber and Magnes.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Kenneth Levin, "Varieties of Jewish Antizionism"
summary: Kenneth Levin argues that Jewish antizionism, from JVP and 'as-a-Jew' critics to institutions embracing BLM and DEI, is a recurring maladaptive response of besieged minorities seeking acceptance by adopting their haters' indictments. He traces this pattern from Enlightenment-era reform through the Pittsburgh Platform and Warburg and Magnes to today, and contends that blaming Israeli policy for antisemitism misdiagnoses the threat to American Jews.
stance: critical of Jewish antizionism and of appeasement-driven Jewish responses to antisemitism
relevance_reason: The essay's central subject is Jewish antizionism, analyzing its forms, historical roots, and psychological drivers.

publication: Institute for Critical Study of Antizionism (ICSA)
title: By Simon Lucas, "The Curious Case of Philosophy's Disciplinary Failure in Addressing Gaza"
summary: The author argues that contemporary moral philosophy has failed to provide rigorous analysis of the Gaza war, relying instead on flawed legal positivism, stipulative reasoning, and moral narration that reflect prior ideological commitments. He attributes this to a 'moral supremacy of victimhood' framework, editorial bias, and social pressures within academia, and says philosophy risks losing its authority unless it restores rigor and epistemic humility.
stance: critical of antizionist moral philosophy and its editorial and ideological structures

He attributes the appeal of both movements to economic scarcity and inequality and urges people to ask whether the angry person with the megaphone actually meets their needs.
stance: critical of both far-right anti-immigration and antizionist 'pro-Palestine' movements
relevance_reason: The post analyzes the 'pro-Palestine' movement in Australia as driven by an antisemitic conception of Zionism and compares it to the far-right anti-immigration movement.

title: A Normal Week
summary: The author recounts a week of activism, media appearances, and community events in Sydney, lamenting that analysis countering disinformation about Israel goes unpublished and that antisemitism is a conspiracy theory rather than only racism. He also describes peace-oriented dialogue events and expresses hope in groups like Women Wage Peace.
stance: Critical of antizionism and of media disinformation about Israel; favors dialogue and peace-building across political divides
relevance_reason: The post is a personal weekly diary by the head of an antizionism-focused movement, covering antizionist activism, antisemitism, media disinformation about Israel, and peace-building responses.

title: "Let them eat state": Is self-determination doomed by the West's tin ear?
summary: The author argues that Australia's cancellation of Israeli MP Simcha Rothman's visa exposes a double standard, since the domestic antizionist movement, which seeks to eliminate the Jewish state, is tolerated and normalised despite being extreme. He also questions Palestinian statehood recognition given Palestinian leadership and public attitudes, and calls for consistent standards on extremism.
stance: critical of the Australian antizionist movement and of the government's inconsistent standards, while also critical of Simcha Rothman and Palestinian leadership
relevance_reason: The post centrally examines the Australian antizionist movement, its goal of eliminating the Jewish state, and the inconsistency in how extremism is defined, with detailed references to APAN and Palestine Action Group.

title: It's August, 2025.
summary: The author recounts, in a non-linear memoir, his path from a Canberra parliamentary career through breakdown, hospitalisation, sobriety and work in construction and landscaping. He ends by describing how October 7th and the reactions of acquaintances, a university peer and artists he admired who celebrated the violence and called for the removal of Jews pushed him to return home to Sydney.
stance: personal memoir, critical of those who celebrated October 7th
relevance_reason: This is a personal memoir about mental illness, recovery and manual labour whose only antizionism-related content is a brief passage on post-October 7 celebration of violence by acquaintances and artists, with the publication's framing implying that is the turning point.

title: Politely dismantling collective punishment.
summary: The author responds to Ginger Gorman's op-ed 'The Great Silence,' arguing that her shame at being Jewish amounts to collective punishment of diaspora Jews and that her Holocaust comparisons are numerically and historically false. He also disputes her claims about genocide, targeting of journalists and 'concentration camps,' and argues that antizionism is by definition opposition to Israel's existence rather than criticism of its actions.
stance: critical of Holocaust inversion and collective punishment of Jews; rebuttal of a specific op-ed, courteous in tone
relevance_reason: The post is a direct rebuttal of an op-ed that uses Holocaust inversion and genocide accusations against Israel, and it defines antizionism as opposition to Israel's existence.

title: Indirect censorship's effect on the brain
summary: The author argues that algorithmic content feeds from companies like Meta, Google, and X act as a form of 'indirect censorship' that shapes thoughts and emotions. He questions whether hate speech produced in such an information environment is truly 'free speech' deserving protection.
stance: critical of social media algorithms and tech companies; questions whether algorithm-driven speech counts as free
relevance_reason: The post is a general essay on algorithmic 'indirect censorship' and free speech/hate speech; antizionism is never mentioned, though it is published in an antizionism-focused newsletter.

title: How does one win a culture war?
summary: The author argues that Australia's post-Howard-era culture wars were fought against targets without a guiding goal (telos), leaving cultural institutions and politicians adrift and prone to treating Jews as part of 'the system' unworthy of protection. He defines antizionism as denying self-determination uniquely to Jews and cites Mehreen Faruqi's call for the Special Envoy's resignation and Jason Clare's Islamophobia comparison as examples of prejudice.
stance: critical of Australian cultural institutions and politicians who fail to confront antisemitism; defends Zionism
relevance_reason: The post directly addresses antizionism, defining it and arguing it is antisemitic, and examines how Australian cultural institutions and politicians respond to antisemitism and antizionism.

title: Hit job on Special Envoy could have been avoided
summary: The author argues that the re-publication of a donation by Special Envoy Jillian Segal's husband's family trust to the lobby group Advance appears timed to undermine her antisemitism recommendations, with anti-Zionist groups like the Jewish Council of Australia echoing APAN's language in response. He also contends the controversy was avoidable, since someone tasked with shaping public opinion should have foreseen the poor optics, and he links antisemitism to conspiratorial ideas about Jewish and Israeli power.
stance: Critical of the attack on Segal and of anti-Zionist groups' coordinated response, while also criticizing Segal's lapse in judgment over the donation
relevance_reason: The post analyzes a coordinated campaign, including by anti-Zionist Jewish groups, to discredit Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism and her recommendations, and discusses antisemitic conspiracy narratives about Jews and Israel.

title: Is yelling "death to the IDF" antisemitic?
summary: The author argues that antisemitism is best understood as a conspiracy theory rather than race-based hatred, and that chants like "death to the IDF" can draw on antisemitic tropes by casting Israel as uniquely evil, even when criticism of Israel as such is legitimate. He supplements this with a historical list of antisemitism's forms and says antizionism aims to annul Israel and echoes older conspiracy narratives.
stance: critical of antizionism and of the Glastonbury performers' rhetoric
relevance_reason: The post directly analyzes when anti-Israel rhetoric (Kneecap and Bob Vylan at Glastonbury) becomes antisemitic and defines antizionism as the effort to annul Israel, tying it to conspiratorial antisemitism.

title: Glastonbury 2025: eating from the trash.
summary: The author argues that Glastonbury 2025 and the BBC's live-streaming of Kneecap and Bob Vylan show antisemitic ideas spreading as fashion, with cultural institutions choosing to cater to the crowd rather than lead. He compares the artists and festivals to fast fashion and contrasts the crowd's chants with the reality of the Nova festival massacre.
stance: critical of Glastonbury, the BBC, and the artists platformed
relevance_reason: The post critiques Glastonbury 2025 and the BBC for platforming Kneecap and Bob Vylan's chants against the IDF, framing this as antisemitism and antizionism travelling through cultural institutions.

title: Reality is not a shared experience
summary: The author uses Kant's noumena/phenomena distinction and a domino metaphor to argue that people experience reality individually and so disagree about shared events. He illustrates this with a fictional antizionist (Elliot) and a Zionist (Sam) whose friendship collapses after October 7, and argues that rigid inherited narratives and consensus-driven history entrench conflict.
stance: philosophical essay on divergent realities, with illustrative sympathy toward the Zionist character and criticism of antizionist rhetoric
relevance_reason: The essay is a philosophical piece on epistemology and subjective reality, using an extended Elliot/Sam fictional vignette about October 7 and antizionism as its main illustration, so antizionism is an example rather than the main subject.

title: An Update from the For Normal People Puppet Mastery Division Writing Room
summary: Framed as a memo from a celestial TV writers' room, the author argues that Westerners prioritise personal emotional gratification over historical and ethical responsibility. He claims this made them susceptible to antisemitism repackaged as Pan-Arab nationalism and to romanticising violence far away, rather than learning from history.
stance: critical of Western progressive/campus fashionable politics and of antisemitism repackaged as anti-colonial solidarity
relevance_reason: Antizionism is touched on only in an allegorical aside (antisemitism repackaged as Pan-Arab nationalism, Western fetishisation of foreign resistance, romanticised distant violence) within a broader satirical critique of Western gratification culture.

title: Trolley Problems for Normal People
summary: The author uses a modified trolley problem to argue that antizionism targets Israel's mere existence rather than its conduct, and that Zionism is a response to that threat. He also traces genocide and Holocaust-inversion rhetoric to Soviet propaganda and October 7, and urges Zionists to define their own limits on how the war is conducted.
stance: self-identified leftist Zionist; opposes antizionism while urging Zionists to reflect critically on Israel's conduct in Gaza
relevance_reason: The post is an extended argument about antizionism as a position against Israel's existence, covering Holocaust inversion, genocide accusations, Soviet propaganda, and the 1968 Polish purge.

title: USYD staff defend right to advocate for "elimination" of Jewish State.
summary: The author reports on a University of Sydney staff forum at which speakers argued against adopting the Universities Australia antisemitism definition, including defending the right to call for the 'elimination' of Israel as free speech. The piece contrasts these views with testimony from Jewish and Israeli staff who described exclusion and an unsafe campus, and notes the near-unanimous vote to reject the definition.
stance: critical of the USYD staff forum's rejection of the antisemitism definition; sympathetic to Jewish staff and the definition
relevance_reason: The post reports on a University of Sydney staff forum rejecting an antisemitism definition and defending calls for the 'elimination' of Israel, squarely about antizionist rhetoric and institutions on campus.

title: Twenty thoughts on language and violence.
summary: The author offers twenty numbered reflections arguing that the war is unwinnable and Hamas must not escape accountability. He holds that 'genocide' and Holocaust analogies are used as rhetorical weapons, that misrepresentation of Zionism has fueled global hostility, and that antisemitism is marked by the language used rather than by pro-Palestinian or anti-Israel sentiment as such.
stance: critical of genocide rhetoric and Holocaust inversion, while also critical of the war and Hamas
relevance_reason: The post substantially addresses the genocide accusation, Holocaust inversion, how Zionism is misrepresented, and how antizionist rhetoric came to justify October 7.

title: Voting against the Greens [pub. AFR election day 2025]
summary: The author argues that Australian Jews face heightened uncertainty on election day amid surging post-October 7 antisemitism, including the exclusion of 'Zionists' from universities and the arts. He says Labor's actions are welcome but its rhetoric lacks conviction, and he fears Greens influence given their hostility to Israel, so he is voting as a Jew first.
stance: critical of the Greens and of Labor's weak rhetoric on antisemitism; explains why he is voting as a Jew first
relevance_reason: The op-ed centres on antizionist exclusion of Jews in Australian arts and universities, Greens hostility to Israel, and how this shapes Jewish voting in the 2025 election.

title: Shrewd campaign ends on terrifying note
summary: The author argues that Memo Review used the Khaled Sabsabi controversy to move from a broad transparency campaign to promoting conspiracy claims about a 'Zionist lobby,' and that Australia's government-funded arts sector enforces a one-sided antizionist orthodoxy through boycotts, cancellations and doxxing of Jewish artists. He contends this goes beyond legitimate concern for Palestinians and resembles Protocols-style conspiratorial thinking.
stance: critical of antizionist conspiracy narratives and boycott culture in the Australian arts sector
relevance_reason: The post is a sustained critique of antizionist rhetoric, conspiracy framing, and boycott culture in the Australian arts sector, centered on the Sabsabi/Creative Australia controversy.

title: Khaled Sabsabi breaks silence.
summary: The author argues that artist Khaled Sabsabi, despite being treated unfairly by Creative Australia's rescinding of his Venice Biennale appointment, belongs to a boycott culture that singles out Israel and Israeli artists, which the author characterises as antisemitic. He also contends that Australia's publicly funded arts sector platforms radicalised artists and that Creative Australia handled the matter clumsily without addressing the underlying problems.
stance: critical of Khaled Sabsabi and the antizionist arts sector, while also critical of Creative Australia's handling
relevance_reason: The post argues that boycotting only the Jewish state and its artists is antisemitic and discusses radicalisation and antizionism in Australia's arts and university sectors.

title: Australia does not censor radicalised artists. [pub. in The Australian 25/2/2025]
summary: The author argues that the arts-sector open letter defending Khaled Sabsabi misrepresents the controversy as government censorship, when the real censorship is artists bullying and doxxing each other, particularly Jewish artists. He contends that Creative Australia funds artists who glorify Hamas and Hezbollah or harass Jews, and calls for more discernment and an overhaul of grant selection processes.
stance: critical of Australia's arts sector, Creative Australia's funding practices, and the Memo Review open letter
relevance_reason: The post examines antizionism and antisemitism in Australia's arts sector, including artist boycotts of Israeli artists, the doxxing of Jewish artists, and glorification of Hamas and Hezbollah by funded artists.

title: Creative Australia - the sum of its parts.
summary: The author argues that Creative Australia has long funded artists who celebrate Hamas and Hezbollah and harass fellow artists, yet its mandate rightly avoids moral arbitration. Using Berlin's two concepts of liberty, the author contends that artists demand the freedom to censor and vilify each other while objecting to Creative Australia exercising a similar power.
stance: critical of artists who harass peers and celebrate terror groups, while also critical of the hypocrisy of the outcry against Creative Australia
relevance_reason: The post addresses antizionist hostility within the Australian arts sector, including artists celebrating Hamas and Hezbollah, doxxing peers and demanding Jews be removed from galleries, and the Creative Australia controversy.

title: We cannot hide from Australia Day [pub. The ABC, Australia Day 2025]
summary: The author reflects on whether Australia Day can be celebrated given unrepaired harm to Indigenous Australians, arguing a good country can hold both pride and shame at once. He rejects the fashionable view of Australia as merely a settler-colonial, genocidal project while acknowledging its failures toward Indigenous people.

relevance_reason: The essay is about Australia Day, Indigenous disadvantage and national shame, and only gestures at antizionism indirectly through the author's family Holocaust background and a brief rejection of the 'settler-colonial, genocidal' framing of Australia.

title: Short: Good morning world
summary: The author reflects on a morning in Sydney marked by antizionist stickers, graffiti, and calls to globalise the intifada, arguing that the supposed distinction between antizionism and antisemitism has collapsed. He cites a news report of cars vandalised with 'fuck Israel' messages and contests the claim that Jewish indigeneity does not ground a land claim.
stance: critical of antizionism; personal essay from a Jewish Australian perspective
relevance_reason: The post is a personal reflection centered on antizionism as a movement, its rhetoric, symbols, and its effect on Jews in Sydney, including a reported antisemitic vandalism incident.

title: Questioning the word 'pogrom'
summary: The author, a Sydney Jew, uses a beach afternoon and the mitzvah on idol worship to wrestle with the Amsterdam beatings of Jewish football fans and whether 'pogrom' is the right word. He questions people who post 'context' to justify the attacks, compares this logic to excuses made for October 7, and asks why Jews are held responsible for Israeli government actions in ways Palestinians are not for Hamas.
stance: personal reflection, distressed by justification of antisemitic violence
relevance_reason: The post reflects on the Amsterdam attacks on Jewish football fans and the justifications offered for them, engaging with antizionist rhetoric, victim-blaming, and the 'Zionist' vs 'Jew' distinction.

title: 2. Would a progressive or a conservative be more likely to cut me in half?
summary: The author, drawing on Mary Midgley's essay on moral relativism and absolutism, argues that Australian progressives uphold universal moral standards against domestic social conservatism but abandon them when asked to condemn Hamas's October 7 attack. He frames this as a selective retreat into moral isolationism when it suits ideological goals, and promises to expand on progressive support for theocratic movements abroad in the next essay.
stance: critical of Australian progressives' selective moral reasoning on Hamas and October 7
relevance_reason: The post argues that Australian progressives apply moral absolutism to domestic social conservatism but shift to moral relativism when excusing Hamas and October 7, which is a critique of antizionism in progressive spaces.

title: 1. What do Australian progressives want, and why?
summary: The author argues that the idea that people mature from progressivism into conservatism is a false adage, and that young Australians, disadvantaged relative to their parents, are driven by a self-imposed desire to repair the world. He cautions Jews not to mistake conservative pandering for authentic representation, setting up a series on Australian progressive ethics.
stance: sympathetic to progressive aims while critical of progressive excesses and of conservative dismissiveness
relevance_reason: This is the first part of a series on Australian progressive ethics that mostly discusses generational politics, conservatism and woke culture, with antizionism appearing only in passing (a SodaStream boycott example and a closing note to Jews about conservative pandering).

title: The difference between civilian and combatant casualties
summary: The author argues that Israel's pager operation against Hezbollah was a justified, precise response to thousands of rocket attacks, and that responsibility for civilian harm lies with terror groups that embed among civilians. He criticizes media omissions and Western pro-Hezbollah sympathizers, including those who rallied in Melbourne, for inverting the moral picture.
suggested_tags: Laws of war and civilian casualties
stance: critical of anti-Israel narratives and Hezbollah sympathizers; defends Israel's targeting of Hezbollah
relevance_reason: The post argues against the moral inversion that casts Israel as terrorist after the Hezbollah pager attacks, criticizing pro-Hezbollah and anti-Israel sentiment among Australian activists and the public.

title: Collateral
summary: The author describes bracing for how antizionists online would turn the Hezbollah pager attack into something Jews must apologise for, arguing antizionism is irreconcilable because it presumes Israel should not exist. He then reflects with regret on posting a celebratory song, concluding that child deaths should not be dismissed as 'collateral' even as Jews have nothing to apologise for.
stance: critical of antizionism; self-critical personal reflection on his own response to the operation
relevance_reason: The essay reflects on antizionist rhetoric and the 'They' who insist on Jewish statelessness, using the Hezbollah pager operation as an occasion, so antizionism is a substantial theme.

title: The Omnicause and the Arts
summary: The author argues that diverse protest causes, including Palestinian solidarity, have fused into an undifferentiated 'omnicause' driven by mass media, algorithms, binary thinking and Western colonial shame, in place of historical understanding. He frames this as a prelude to a second part claiming the omnicause stifles creativity and lets artists gain reputation from global tragedies.
stance: critical of the omnicause and performative activism
relevance_reason: The essay analyzes the 'omnicause' (antizionism and Palestinian solidarity fused into a broad protest movement) and previews a follow-up on its effect on the arts, on a publication devoted to antizionism.

title: For how long will Australians make excuses for antisemitism?
summary: The author argues that Australians, including young progressives, are excusing antisemitic behaviour, such as an Officeworks manager refusing to serve a Jewish customer, as 'antizionism, not antisemitism'. Drawing on personal examples of learning that ignorance or good intentions don't excuse harmful conduct, he calls on non-Jews to educate and hold others accountable rather than make excuses.
stance: critical of antisemitic conduct excused as antizionism; urges non-Jews to challenge it
relevance_reason: The essay directly addresses the line between antizionism and antisemitism, using an Australian incident where a Jewish customer was refused service to argue that 'pro-Palestine' ideology is being used to justify antisemitic conduct.

title: Jillian Segal's one job
summary: The author argues that Zionism is simply the acknowledgement of Jewish indigeneity and Israel's legitimacy as a state, and that most people, including campus activists, do not know what the word means. He contends that the new antisemitism envoy's real task is to address antisemitism as a conspiracy theory and the obsession with Jewish statelessness, starting with defining Zionism publicly.
stance: Zionist, critical of antizionism and of the Jewish Council's stance, supportive of Segal's remit
relevance_reason: The post centers on defining Zionism, Jewish indigeneity, and the need for Australia's antisemitism envoy to confront rejection of Israel's legitimacy, drawing on the author's encounters with antizionism at campus encampments.

title: The Egocentric Humanitarian
summary: The author argues that much zealous humanitarian politics, including the rush to condemn Israel after October 7, stems from egocentrism, shame and a need for absolution rather than genuine understanding. Drawing on his own past as a moralizing activist and his rehab experience, he urges readers to examine their motives and temper zeal with humility and curiosity.
stance: critical of performative, ego-driven activism, including antizionist reactions to Oct 7; self-reflective memoir
relevance_reason: The essay is a personal reflection on how zealous, ego-driven online activism around the Israel-Gaza conflict is rooted in shame and unmet needs, touching antizionist rhetoric ('act of resistance', 'colonial oppressor', 'genocidal') only as background rather than analyzing antizionism directly.

title: The Colour of Shame
summary: The author argues that Western liberal antizionism is driven by a collective 'shame-body' over colonial history, Soviet propaganda, and ignorance of history, rather than by facts. He contends that Arab antisemitism and rejection of Israel's existence, not Israel's creation, underlie the conflict and the Palestinian refugee crisis.
suggested_tags: Mizrahi Jews and Jewish expulsions from Arab lands
stance: critical of antizionism and of Western liberal responses to Israel; sympathetic to Palestinians but blames Arab states and Hamas
relevance_reason: The essay is centrally about antizionism, arguing that Western liberal reactions to Israel stem from shame and Soviet propaganda and that Arab antisemitism underlies the conflict.

title: American Intellectual Antisemitism
summary: Shai Davidai describes his failed attempt to get Columbia's leadership to confront pro-Hamas campus activism after Oct 7, and argues that an academic ideology he calls 'American Intellectual Antisemitism' recast Jews as privileged oppressors and rationalized the massacre. He presents his book as tracing how this ideology spread from universities into media, K-12 education, and politics, and urges moral clarity and accountability in response.
stance: critical of academic antizionism and university leadership; advocacy for moral clarity and accountability
relevance_reason: The essay is a guest piece by Shai Davidai presenting his book on the ideology and academic roots of antizionist and anti-Jewish thought in American universities and the post-Oct 7 campus response.
